SA Pilot Jeremy Ascough & One Last Orbit

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
SA pilot smashes record flying around the world via the poles

Unique Selling Point:
International Crew, called One More Orbit, set off in July to honour the Apollo 11 moon landing 50 years go - by attempting to break the world record of circumnavigating the earth via the poles.. in the fastest time ever. The record stood at 52 hours set in 2018. it was not officially recorded by the Guiness Book of Records which listed a Boeing 747 making the time in 54 hours. It was an international crew but one of the pilots was SA Jeremy Ascough, a capt for Qatar Airlines. The team broke the record by almost 6 hours.

Summary:
As above..... footage will be supplied by the One More Orbit team. and to help with the narrative we will interview Terry Virtz who was part of the crew. he is an international space staton commander, and Janicke Mikkelson from Norway whose task was to coordinate satelite feeds for live streaming. 3 stops were scheduled and these needed to be done very fast so that the record could be broken. The times of the stops wwre 37 min, 40 min, and 37 minutes

Script:


It was called ONE MORE ORBIT – an international flight crew’s (40 000 kilometre attempt) in July to break the record for the fastest circumnavigation of the earth, via the north and south poles.

ACCORDING TO The Guinness book of World Records, THE FASTEST TIME WAS 54 hours and 7 minutes - set in 1997 by a Pam-Am Boeing 747. a Bombardier jet in 2008 beat that time by almost 2 hours, but Guinness hadn’t officially timed the effort.

For ONE MORE ORBIT, South African pilot Jeremy Ascough was invited to join the crew.

Jeremy: That was an extraordinary feeling, I phone my wife and said this is an opportunity – how can I say no.

The wheels lifted off at 9-32-am on the dot. (on the 9th july)

DEREK
9.32 AM – THAT’S THE EXACT TIME 50 YEARS AGO WHEN APPOLLO 11 LIFTED OFF FROM EARTH – DESTINATION THE MOON

The ONE MORE ORBIT mission was to honour this historical event and for Ascough who lives between Cape town and Qatar it would be the highlight of his aviation career.

His interest in flying started at the tender age of 3 when his adoptive parents took him to an air-show and he boarded a helicopter.

JERRY: And I remember looking between the 2 seats…at the instrument panel in front of me... and that was my decision made…I never wanted to do anything else.

Ascough has flown many dignitaries around Africa – including President Mandela. Today he’s a senior captain for the executive wing of Qatar airlines. It was this airline that was approached to help break the record because of its world wide infrastructure. IT GULSTREAM G 650 ER Executive jets are THE FASTEST AIRLINERS IN THE WORLD.
\

LINK: PUTTING TOGETHER AN ADVENTURE LIKE THIS DOESN’T HAPPEN OVER NIGHT. IT INVOLVED MONTHS OF PLANNING. RIGHT DOWN TO THE VERY LAST DETAIL.

The crew consisted of team leader Capt. Hamish Harding, three Qatar pilots, including Ascough, a flight attendant and a Qatar engineer. Also, on board would be Terry Virtz

Terry: I was excited about this. I have done a lot of other cool things, but this was unique.

Virtz is (was) a colonel in the US air force, a trained fighter pilot – and he was commander of the international space station for a 7month stint. As a celebrated space photographer, HE WOULD BE documenting THE EVENT.


The final crew member was technical wizard Jannicke Mikkelsen from Poland, an award-winning FILM MAKER who would oversee the the live streaming of the journey


Jannicke : it meant a lot to me that my skillsets were valued to achieve this around the world trip.

Link: ANYTHING COULD GO WRING TO SPOIL THE TEAMS ATTEMPT – THE WEATHER, A WARNING LIGHT IN THE COCKPIT, A MECHENICAL PROBLEM---BUT WHAT WOULD BE VITAL WOULD BE THE NASCCAR STYLE PITSTOPS REQUIRED FOR REFUELLING.

Three refuelling stops were scheduled en route. Quick turn-around times would be key to breaking the record.

“One hour to tale off” up sound

On July 9th, with the control room in Qatar watching on, it was time to take off. (from kennedy space centre?)?

Jeremy: Obviously the adrenaline was overwhelming. It was now do or die.

“ready for take-off, you are cleared. runway 311” up sound

Music swells

The flight to the north pole took 7 hours and 38 minutes. Ascough would never forget the moment.

Jeremey it was beautiful, clear day. Lots of ice...amazing to think that I was at the top of the world.

The flight to the Astana International Airport in Kazakhstan, took 4 hrs 37 minutes. Refuelling took exactly 37 minutes.

COL. GENNADY PADALKA, also an international space station commanderder joined the team in kazastan for the rest of the flight.


8 hours and 42 minutes later, Ascough made the landing in Mauritius. Refuelling time: 40 minutes. For Virtz, these stops were the biggest headache.

Terry: The fuel stops were critical so for two reasons. First of all, everybody is rushing so if they make a mistake, they can break the plane so you can’t take off or you take off something bad could happen so they really had to focus on doing things right even though they were in a hurry. And then the other thing is if they do go slowly, we would not have set the record.

Mauritius to Chile took 13 hours and 22 minutes. This was the most dangerous part of the flight – over the south pole, where temperatures had plummeted to -83 degrees Celcius.

Jeremy - 80 degrees is the limitation on our aircraft, so we had to descend to warm air.

Virtz: There were no airfields for diversions, so if something went wrong, we would have to come all the way back to south Africa or head on to Chile – those were really long divert legs!

In the meantime, Mikkelsen’s challenge was to coordinate different satellite companies to ensure livestreaming further north and south on the globe than had ever been achieved before. With fatigue setting in, the team needed a cheerleader – and Ascough was unflagging.

Jannicke: And Jerry was just this upbeat person, like no matter what happened he was just the one that was making everybody smile, everybody laugh, just keeping the atmosphere up and every time we would feel a bit depressed about something he was going " we are flying around the world, we are the fastest people ever" You know he kept reminding us of what we are achieving.

The stop in Chile took 37 minutes. With no mishaps, the crew knew that they would have the record in the bag – barring any unforeseen catastrophe.

The trip back to Kennedy space centre took 10 hours, 6 min. The gulf stream touched down at 12.12 am. A new record had been set – they had done it in only 46 hours and 42 minutes, at an average speed of 860 kpm (??? what does the acronym stand for?) , almost 6 hours faster than the previous record

Up sound : Hamish Harding – We have a wots record, well done team, well done tea.

The moment overwhelmed Ascough and his co-pilot.

Jeremy : When we eventually put the brakes on, we looked at each other- there was a silent moment in the flight deck, and we were both very emotional – a few tears of joy

Jannicke: He came back to the aircraft and he gave us all a big hug and I just hung onto Jerry and he goes are you okay and I was like no, I’m not okay and then we both started crying and getting emotional.

Mikkelsen and Magdalena Starowicz, the flight attended, had become the first women to ever circumnavigate the poles. Ascough’s wife Magdalena had followed the livestream.

Magdalena: It was out of this world; it was unbelievable to meet the people that was there. To see how they all felt, how they all worked. I cannot describe how I felt. Such pride, proud about this. It was fantastic.

On the same day the team received official recognition for their feat from the Guinness book of world records team.

Records.

VIRTZ: From my perspective it was not only about the record… It was using that to talk about the as a vehicle to talk about exploration, the environment and about the international cooperation we had.

(and) A few days later , in Austria, the team was honoured by the Living Legends of Aviation.

Back in Cape Town Ascough was still on a high – his only regret…that his late parents - who had set him up for this destiny, could not celebrate with him.

Jeremy: Unfortunately, they were not there to see the achievements I have done and have had in my aviation career, but it would have been so special if they had been here for this. But they are watching.
